claims.text: R0637's research profile is in electromagnetic compatibility, PCB radiation, signal integrity, pre-compliance EMI, FDTD modelling and near-field scanning, with a group that regularly uses a vector network analyser, near-field scanning bench and FDTD/MoM solvers.
limitations: Profile text is self-described expertise; it does not by itself prove fit to Nexara's specific 150–450 MHz failures.
Evidence snapshot is not semantically assessed.

claims.text: R0637 co-authored work on a rule-based PCB layout scoring tool that ingests Gerber files and a netlist, flags geometric emission-risk violations under 17 rules, and was validated on 23 boards of known emission performance with 83% sensitivity and 22% false-positive rate; the authors describe it as an early design gate, not a replacement for simulation or pre-compliance measurement.
limitations: Validation was against CISPR 22 Class B results on 23 boards; not verified for Nexara's board types, frequency range or class limits.
Reported sensitivity/false-positive figures come from that study only and are not guaranteed to transfer.

claims.text: R0637 co-authored an integrated pre-compliance workflow that sequences layout rule checking, near-field scanning at 3 mm standoff and FDTD simulation; across four prototype boards with two regional companies it identified the dominant emission source in each case, and corrective measures reduced peak radiated emission by 5.2–11.7 dB with 2.1 fewer test-and-rework cycles versus a historical baseline.
limitations: Four-board sample developed with two partner companies; not Nexara's designs or Budapest lab.
Improvements were measured at the pre-compliance receiver, not formal OATS certification outcomes.

claims.text: R0637 co-authored a study showing near-field scan data at 3 mm standoff gave 85% rank-ordering agreement with accredited 3 m OATS results at each board's emission maximum, with absolute amplitude within ±4.5 dB in 74% of cases, degrading to ±9 dB above 700 MHz; the authors frame it as early design triage, not a certification substitute.
limitations: Seven consumer electronics boards; standoff and grid parameters matter and are not guaranteed to apply to Nexara's boards.
Accuracy stated is not a guarantee of passing accredited measurement.

claims.text: R0637 co-authored measurement and simulation work on power delivery network impedance showing a distributed ceramic decoupling strategy reduced peak PDN impedance from 840 mΩ to 210 mΩ at 480 MHz and gave a 4.8 dB reduction in broadband radiated noise floor between 400 and 600 MHz on a test vehicle.
limitations: Single FPGA/ADC test vehicle; results are design-specific and not a general PDN rule for Nexara's boards.
This addresses PDN-related emissions only, not the full 150–450 MHz failure space.

claims.text: R0637 co-authored method-of-moments work showing a 1 mm ground-plane moat increased peak radiated field by 7.4 dB at 600 MHz without bridging, reduced to 1.8 dB with a single 100 nF bridging capacitor, with limits of the analytical approximation above 800 MHz.
limitations: Canonical two-layer board with 50 Ω microstrip and 200 MHz clock; not a general prediction of arbitrary layouts.
Pertinent to return-path discontinuities, one of several possible mechanisms behind Nexara's failures.

claims.text: Taken together, R0637's evidence supports building Nexara a repeatable pre-signoff emission-risk triage: an automated Gerber/netlist rule-score gate plus PDN and return-path checks, escalated to near-field scanning and FDTD only for flagged hotspots. That is a plausible route to catching hotspots during layout review, but the published accuracies are study-specific and the 150–450 MHz band and Nexara's class limits would need re-validation on Nexara's own five boards.
limitations: None of the published validation used Nexara hardware or the Budapest accredited lab; transferability is unverified.
Evidence does not establish that any single tool explains all three failures.

claims.text: Proposed bounded pilot: (1) under NDA, retrospectively run the open rule-checker on Nexara's five boards' Gerber files and netlists, comparing scores against known pass/fail and pre-compliance scan data; (2) for the three failed boards, apply PDN-impedance and return-path/moat checks to the flagged regions; (3) near-field scan only the identified hotspots at the faculty bench where access permits; (4) distill the discriminative checks into a documented layout checklist and a step-by-step simulation workflow for Nexara engineers to run themselves.
limitations: Retrospective scoring on five boards is a small sample and may not be statistically conclusive.
Scanning bench access is cost-recovery and subject to faculty teaching commitments; timing cannot be promised.
If retrospective triage does not separate failing from passing boards, the checklist must be revised or the pilot stopped.

claims.text: Validation plan: baseline is Nexara's current process (HyperLynx impedance checks plus pre-compliance scans) and the historical 3-of-5 first-submission failure record; measurements would be retrospective pass/fail agreement of the rule score on the five boards in 150–450 MHz, hotspot location agreement with near-field scans, and residual PDN impedance/moat-penalty checks versus design intent. Proposed go/no-go: proceed to a prospective checklist release only if the retrospective triage flags the known failures with an acceptable false-positive rate agreed with Nexara; otherwise revise rules.
limitations: Proposed thresholds and milestones are assumptions to confirm jointly, not source facts.
Historical baseline figures come from Nexara's own account and are not independently verified.
Pass criteria must not be framed as guaranteeing accredited-lab success.

claims.text: Participation constraints to confirm: Nexara provides Gerber files, BOM/netlist and pre-compliance scan data for the five boards under NDA; the work is framed as contract research on PCB EMC characterisation and pre-compliance testing. R0637's declared availability is contract research, EMC design-review consulting, joint academic–industrial projects and cost-recovery equipment access; she prefers longer-term projects with real hardware, and the two doctoral students defending in 2026–2027 may limit her time. Committed staff, lab hours and budget are not established here.
limitations: No confirmed availability, budget or schedule for the scanning bench or FDTD licences.
Individual participation consent, NDA terms and data handling arrangements are unresolved.

claims.text: Boundaries: the evidence covers radiated-emission prediction, PDN impedance, return-path discontinuities and near-field triage, which aligns with the 150–450 MHz failure mode, but it does not cover full HyperLynx-based emissions flow configuration, accredited CISPR class-limit sign-off, or every failure mechanism (e.g. cable/harness and enclosure effects) that can drive Budapest failures. Establishing that a checklist reduces re-test cost and delay is a prospective claim that must be verified within the company's own process.
limitations: No evidence in this bundle about EMC labs, CISPR classes or failure mechanisms specific to Nexara.
Remaining requirements outside the tool's scope must be identified with Nexara during the pilot.

summary.text: R0637 is the best-supported candidate: her recorded work spans automated Gerber-based emission-risk rule checking, near-field-scan triage versus accredited OATS results, PDN impedance control and return-path discontinuity modelling, which maps onto Nexara's need to catch 150–450 MHz emission hotspots at layout review rather than after lab failure.
The fit is partial and unverified on Nexara's hardware; the pilot is designed to test whether those methods actually discriminate Nexara's passing and failing boards before any checklist is released.

technicalRationale.text: The rule-checker provides an early layout gate on Gerber/netlist geometry, while the published workflow adds near-field scanning and FDTD quantification only for flagged hotspots, matching Nexara's stated preference for a self-run workflow over per-board consultancy.
PDN impedance and ground-plane moat findings give concrete physical mechanisms and candidate checks for the frequency band of interest, though each was validated on non-Nexara vehicles.

cooperationScope.text: Contribution: retrospective triage of Nexara's five boards with the open rule-checker, PDN and return-path checks, targeted near-field scanning of flagged hotspots, and delivery of a documented layout checklist and simulation workflow with a worked example per failed board.

Milestones (proposed, to confirm): data handover under NDA; baseline reproducibility check; retrospective scoring and hotspot analysis on the three failed boards; checklist draft reviewed with Nexara engineers; final workflow handover and training session.

validation.text: Baseline: Nexara's current HyperLynx impedance checks plus in-house pre-compliance scans and the recorded 3-of-5 first-submission failure history. Measurements: per-board rule score versus known pass/fail, hotspot location agreement with pre-compliance/near-field data, and PDN impedance and moat-penalty indicators on flagged regions.

Proposed go/no-go: release the checklist to Nexara engineers only if retrospective triage flags the known failures with a false-positive rate agreed in advance; otherwise revise or abandon. Track subsequent first-submission outcomes as the real test, without promising accredited-lab success.

constraints.text: Required inputs: Gerber files, BOM/netlist and pre-compliance scan data for the five boards, plus the target class limits and frequency band, all under NDA.

Participation conditions: work framed as contract research/EMC design-review collaboration; scanning bench available only on cost-recovery terms when teaching commitments permit; budget, lab hours and schedule are not established and must be agreed.

unknowns.text: Open questions: which mechanisms dominate the three failures; whether HyperLynx workflows at Nexara can be reconfigured for emissions prediction or a separate FDTD route is needed; whether R0637's bench access and doctoral supervision load permit near-field scanning; and whether results transfer to the Budapest lab's class limits.

findings.explanation: The same publication (SYN-PUB-01515, title E091) is registered as content in both R0637's bundle (identity via E181, author 0) and R0115's bundle (identity via E033, author 1), yet the abstract E047 is identical for both. This is consistent with a multi-author paper, but the bundle's contentLinks list each candidate as author of the same content evidence without indicating relative contribution. Any proposal leaning on this single workflow paper for both candidates cannot be treated as independent corroboration; the two candidates' contributions to the rule-checker, near-field and FDTD components are not separable from the registered evidence.

R0115's own profile evidence describes high-voltage insulation engineering: fields High-Voltage Engineering / Electrical Insulation Technology (E155), bio on medium-voltage insulator field modelling and a high-voltage/salt-fog lab (E138), and industry experience with distribution network operators on insulator selection (E053). Of R0115's content evidence only the co-authored E047 (SYN-PUB-01515) and E186 (single-phase inverter conducted emissions 150 kHz–2 MHz) touch EMC; E125 (insulator field prediction with ML) and E133/E182 are insulator work. Nothing in the registered evidence shows radiated-emission PCB layout review capability beyond a shared co-authorship, and equipment access (E005) is high-voltage/salt-fog, not radiated-emission measurement. Technical suitability for the 150–450 MHz radiated-emissions layout workflow is therefore not established by this candidate's own profile.

R0690 is an electronic-test-engineering profile: boundary-scan/in-circuit test, DFT test coverage, thermal-cycling degradation (E087, E101, E048, E111, E003, E160, E144, E096, E086). The lexical overlap with the challenge comes from generic words such as 'layout', 'checklist', 'boards', 'test'. No registered evidence addresses radiated emissions, EMC limits, or emission hotspot prediction; her test lab equipment (E077, E146) is boundary-scan, flying-probe and thermal cycling. For the specific need (predict and fix 150–450 MHz radiated hotspots during layout review), support is not established.

R0611's evidence base is conducted emission and power-quality/network modelling: LISN reprodibility for SMPS (E174/E121), EV on-board-charger conducted disturbance propagation (E079/E011), LED driver conducted emission modelling (E149), ripple-control/supraharmonic interference (E030), a book chapter on low-voltage distribution EMC (E049), and keywords dominated by conducted emissions (E023). Her open_to (E161) offers LISN-based conducted emission measurement and network impedance to 30 MHz — 30 MHz upper limit is below the 150–450 MHz radiated band the company needs, and none of her registered evidence addresses radiated field emission from digital PCB layout.

R0587 fits EMC pre-compliance testing, but the registered evidence is centred on 30–300 MHz near-field/OATS correlation that degrades above 500 MHz (E129: accuracy worsened above 500 MHz due to spatial aliasing; E056), LoRa/EN 301 489 device testing at 500–1000 MHz (E112), chamber/lab intercomparison and uncertainty budgets (E122, E040), and antenna/RED compliance consulting (E066, E035). His stated preference (E162) is collaborating with IoT/wireless companies on EU market entry and on topics suitable for student theses rather than routine testing. There is no registered evidence of a documented layout-checklist or simulation workflow that a company's own engineers could run; the 150–450 MHz band of interest sits in the weaker-accuracy region of his own cited method.

R0660's work is GaN/wide-bandgap converter characterisation: common-source inductance PCB studies (E016/E130), a 1 MHz GaN DC–DC EMI characterisation including radiated measurement in a semi-anechoic chamber (E018/E165), and double-pulse/calorimetric benches. His open_to (E036) and notes (E150) target power-electronics companies and measurement tasks his GaN laboratory is equipped for, and he is described as cautious about travel during semester. The radiated-emission content is for a switching converter, not general digital/mixed-signal PCB layout prediction at 150–450 MHz, and no registered evidence shows a repeatable emissions-prediction workflow deliverable.

R0182's only radiated-emission item is a co-authored (author 3) FDTD stack-up sensitivity study on a benchmark 500 MHz clock tree (E100/E145/E019); everything else is surge protective devices, lightning protection, PV installations and spectrum-occupancy work (E099, E017, E153, E028). His profile has an empty bio, his open_to (E034) is SPD/PV/lightning oriented, and notes (E115) state shared, pre-booked impulse-lab access and limited capacity for a third doctoral student until mid-2027. Support for a radiated-emission layout workflow is thin and co-authorship does not establish his role in it.

R0283's profile is conducted EMI in variable-speed drives: EMC input filter sizing for IEC 61800-3 Category C2 (E176/E022), DC-link ESL effects on conducted emissions (E109), PE-impedance dependent CM attenuation (E104), motor-cable CM emissions (E009), and a drive-EMC book chapter (E070). Her notes (E042) target drive/frequency-converter/integration companies with IEC 61800-3 challenges, and her equipment offer is an EMI receiver and LISN under a formal agreement. None of the registered evidence addresses radiated emissions from digital PCB layout at 150–450 MHz or a layout-review prediction workflow.

Even for the best-matching candidate R0637, the cited methods state accuracy limits relevant to the company's 150–450 MHz problem: the Gerber rule-scoring tool reports 83% sensitivity and a 22% false-positive rate and is described as an early design gate rather than a replacement for simulation or measurement (E006); near-field-to-far-field prediction degrades to ±9 dB above 700 MHz and is characterised as early-design triage (E135); the integrated workflow was validated on four prototype boards in collaboration with two companies and reduced peak emissions 5.2–11.7 dB pre-OATS (E047). These are research-prototype validations, not evidence that a maintainable checklist/simulation workflow already exists for the company's own engineers across varied board types. The rule-checker code is described as deposited in an open repository (E047), but maintenance, HyperLynx integration and hand-over to the company are not evidenced by the registered text.

Across all eight candidates the registered restrictions show a mix of engagement forms and limits that bear on the company's explicit 'no per-board consultancy' and 'run it themselves' requirement: R0637's bench is only available when teaching commitments permit (E132) and her model is contract research/consulting (E025); R0587 prefers thesis-generating collaborations (E066); others offer generic 'consulting' (E005, E146, E170, E161) or narrow, pre-booked equipment access (E034). None of the registered restrictions states a commitment to deliver an engineer-operable, maintainable in-house workflow, so a Proposer claim that any candidate will transfer a self-service workflow is not supported by the restriction text alone.

Every bundle carries IDENTITY_UNRESOLVED diagnostics: co-authors on each publication have no internal researcher ID and are not merged. Author positions vary widely (for example R0283 and R0611 appear as author 4, author 2 or author 3 on several items; R0182 as author 3 on the only radiated-emission paper; R0587 as author 2 on the near-field/OATS paper). First/individual-level contribution cannot be inferred from position alone and no registered evidence states which parts of a co-authored study a given candidate performed. This limits how strongly any candidate's specific technical role can be attributed.

findings.explanation: The draft attributes the key publications to R0637 by co-authorship, which is accurate, but the phrasing 'co-authored work on...' with C7/C8 built on them should stay attentive to author position: E110 places her at author index 3 (last) on the rule-checker paper SYN-PUB-07261, where the abstract says the tool was 'implemented in Python' without attributing specific components. By contrast E181 (author 0) on SYN-PUB-01515, E057 (author 0) on SYN-PUB-07041, E039 (author 0) on SYN-PUB-07040, E092 (author 0) on SYN-PUB-07257, and project participation E094 (principal investigator, SYN-PRJ-0366, E064) do support a leading role on the workflow project. No claim states she invented a named component, and the study-specific limitations are declared, so this is not a false inference; the advisory note is that the retrospective pilot (C8) should not implicitly assume her authorship-level ownership of rules she may have only co-reviewed, and training/handover commitments remain unestablished (C10 already says so).
findings.recheckQuestion: If revised, does the text avoid implying that R0637 personally authored or can hand over undocumented internals of the rule-checker (where she is author 3, E110), relying instead on the openly deposited code (E047) and her PI role in SYN-PRJ-0366 (E064/E094)?

findings.explanation: C7 recommends 'PDN and return-path checks' then escalation to near-field scanning and FDTD as catching hotspots 'during layout review' for the 150–450 MHz band. The supporting sources are narrower in frequency: the PDN evidence (E007) reports a 4.8 dB noise-floor reduction only over 400–600 MHz on one FPGA/ADC vehicle, and the moat study (E075) quantifies a 7.4 dB penalty at 600 MHz (third harmonic of a 200 MHz clock), outside or at the top edge of the 150–450 MHz band; the near-field evidence (E135) gives rank agreement at each board's maximum with ±4.5 dB and degradation only above 700 MHz but was validated on seven consumer boards. C7 already labels these as study-specific and C9 makes retrospective 150–450 MHz agreement the go/no-go test, so no unsupported guarantee is made; the advisory point is that the mechanism coverage inside 150–450 MHz rests on plan-to-validate rather than on existing per-frequency measurements, which the pilot design correctly targets.
findings.recheckQuestion: Does C7/C9 keep the 150–450 MHz within-band validation explicitly as an open pilot objective (not an already-demonstrated result), given E007's 400–600 MHz and E075's 600 MHz scope?

findings.explanation: SYN-PUB-01515 (E047) is registered as content for both R0637 (E181, author 0) and R0115 (E033, author 1). The draft cites it only for R0637, where author-0 position and her PI role on the linked project (E064) make the attribution the strongest available; the shared listing does not weaken C3's factual content statements about four prototype boards, two partner companies, 5.2–11.7 dB reduction and 2.1 fewer cycles, all of which are quoted directly from E047 and bounded in C3's limitations. No cross-candidate independence claim is made in the draft, so this is informational.
findings.recheckQuestion: Does the draft avoid using E047 as independent corroboration across candidates or as evidence of R0637's exclusive ownership of the workflow?

findings.explanation: C8/C10 correctly record that near-field scanning bench access is cost-recovery and subject to teaching commitments (E132) and that work is framed as contract research (E025), consistent with the registered open_to text; the company's request for a self-run workflow rather than per-board consultancy is addressed by deliverables (documented checklist plus step-by-step workflow, C8) and the milestones in cooperationScope. What is genuinely unresolved is commercial terms, lab hours and NTech/Nexara-side equipment and licensing (HyperLynx vs FDTD), and the draft lists these as unknowns rather than asserting availability. This is honestly labeled uncertainty, not a defect, and no participation restriction in E025/E132/E137 is violated.
findings.recheckQuestion: Do C8/C10 keep cost, schedule and licence provisions as items to be agreed, without stating them as committed availability?

claims.text: R0637's research profile is in electromagnetic compatibility, PCB radiation, signal integrity, pre-compliance EMI, FDTD modelling and near-field scanning, with a group that regularly uses a vector network analyser, near-field scanning bench and FDTD/MoM solvers.
limitations: Profile text is self-described expertise; it does not by itself prove fit to Nexara's specific 150–450 MHz failures.

claims.text: R0637 co-authored work on a rule-based PCB layout scoring tool that ingests Gerber files and a netlist, flags geometric emission-risk violations under 17 rules, and was validated on 23 boards of known emission performance with 83% sensitivity and 22% false-positive rate; the authors describe it as an early design gate, not a replacement for simulation or pre-compliance measurement.
limitations: Validation was against CISPR 22 Class B results on 23 boards; not verified for Nexara's board types, frequency range or class limits.
Reported sensitivity/false-positive figures come from that study only and are not guaranteed to transfer.

claims.text: R0637 co-authored an integrated pre-compliance workflow that sequences layout rule checking, near-field scanning at 3 mm standoff and FDTD simulation; across four prototype boards with two regional companies it identified the dominant emission source in each case, and corrective measures reduced peak radiated emission by 5.2–11.7 dB with 2.1 fewer test-and-rework cycles versus a historical baseline.
limitations: Four-board sample developed with two partner companies; not Nexara's designs or Budapest lab.
Improvements were measured at the pre-compliance receiver, not formal OATS certification outcomes.

claims.text: R0637 co-authored a study showing near-field scan data at 3 mm standoff gave 85% rank-ordering agreement with accredited 3 m OATS results at each board's emission maximum, with absolute amplitude within ±4.5 dB in 74% of cases, degrading to ±9 dB above 700 MHz; the authors frame it as early design triage, not a certification substitute.
limitations: Seven consumer electronics boards; standoff and grid parameters matter and are not guaranteed to apply to Nexara's boards.
Accuracy stated is not a guarantee of passing accredited measurement.

claims.text: R0637 co-authored measurement and simulation work on power delivery network impedance showing a distributed ceramic decoupling strategy reduced peak PDN impedance from 840 mΩ to 210 mΩ at 480 MHz and gave a 4.8 dB reduction in broadband radiated noise floor between 400 and 600 MHz on a test vehicle.
limitations: Single FPGA/ADC test vehicle; results are design-specific and not a general PDN rule for Nexara's boards.
This addresses PDN-related emissions only, not the full 150–450 MHz failure space.

claims.text: R0637 co-authored method-of-moments work showing a 1 mm ground-plane moat increased peak radiated field by 7.4 dB at 600 MHz without bridging, reduced to 1.8 dB with a single 100 nF bridging capacitor, with limits of the analytical approximation above 800 MHz.
limitations: Canonical two-layer board with 50 Ω microstrip and 200 MHz clock; not a general prediction of arbitrary layouts.
Pertinent to return-path discontinuities, one of several possible mechanisms behind Nexara's failures.

claims.text: Taken together, R0637's evidence supports building Nexara a repeatable pre-signoff emission-risk triage: an automated Gerber/netlist rule-score gate plus PDN and return-path checks, escalated to near-field scanning and FDTD only for flagged hotspots. That is a plausible route to catching hotspots during layout review, but the published accuracies are study-specific and the 150–450 MHz band and Nexara's class limits would need re-validation on Nexara's own five boards.
limitations: None of the published validation used Nexara hardware or the Budapest accredited lab; transferability is unverified.
